name: Rongga
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Arka, I Wayan, Jeladu Kosmas & I Nyoman Suparsa. 2007. Bahasa Rongga: Tatabahasa Acuan Ringkas. Jakarta: Penerbit Universitas Atma Jaya (PUAJ). xii+243 pp. [phonology chapter drafted by Suparsa]. Open scan:https://eprints.unmas.ac.id/682/2/EBK-00400.pdf
catalog_quote: Bahasa Rongga bukan bahasa bertekanan (stress language). Tekanan (stress) tidak bersifat fungsional fonemis. Artinya, kata yang sama dengan tekanan pada suku kata yang berbeda tidak menimbulkan perbedaan makna. Walapun demikian, dalam irama intonasi alamiah, suku kata dalam kata, frasa, atau kalimat diberi tekanan yang tidak sama. ... Pola tekanan kata dalam bahasa Rongga diperlihatkan pada (2-35). Secara umum dapat dikatakan, tekanan utama biasanya ada pada suku terakhir (2-35)a,c, kecuali pada kata yang bersuku dua, yang biasanya ada variasi dengan tekanan yang biasanya pada suku pertama, atau kedua dari belakang (2-35)b. (2-35) Pola tekanan kata pada kata dasar bahasa Rongga: (σ=suku kata, '=bertekanan) a. Kata bersukukata satu: [σ'] (mis. dhu' 'particle') b. Kata bersukukata dua: [σ'σ] (mis. bha'.bha 'marah') c. Kata bersukukata tiga atau lebih: [(σ)σσσ'] (mis. ga.ra.gem' 'bunyi burung dara' fa.ra.ge.ge' 'laba-laba'). Kata yang merupakan kata majemuk (terbanyak bersuku kata empat, terdiri atas dua sub-kata) tidak menunjukkan kosistensi tekanan kata. Pola tekanannya biasanya menuruti pola yang ditunjukkan pada (2-35). Jadi masing-masing kata pembentuknya ada tekanannya, dan salah satu menjadi tekanan utama kata majemuk bersangkutan, dan yang lainnya menjadi tekanan sekunder. Setidak-tidaknya ada dua pola yang dapat dilihat seperti yang ditunjukkan oleh (2-36), walapun harus diakui ada variasi yang lain.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: The findings of compression placement on Rongga reveal that firstly, the monosyllabic words, whether or not preceded by a consonant, whether or not preceded by a consonant stressed on a single syllable and whether or not preceded by a consonant or before the second syllable, both of which either precedes the consonant or do not follow a word boundary. Second, three and four monosyllabic words will be stressed on the last syllable if they precede the consonant or not.
new_statements.translation: Best-effort de-garbling (NOT reliable): 'Stress ("compression" = tekanan) placement in Rongga: (i) in monosyllables the single syllable is stressed whether or not it has an onset consonant, and [in disyllables] the vowel before the second [= final] syllable is stressed, whether or not an onset precedes, before the word boundary; (ii) three- and four-syllable words are stressed on the last syllable [or: counted from the last syllable?] whether or not an onset precedes.'
new_statements.citation: Suparsa, I Nyoman. 2020 (Vol. 11 No. 4, 2021). "The phonological process of Rongga language from the phonemic into phonetic realization." Journal of Cultural Heritage Management and Sustainable Development 11(4):427-439. Emerald. DOI 10.1108/JCHMSD-01-2020-0012.
new_statements.locator: Structured abstract, 'Findings' paragraph (publisher landing page; identical text in Semantic Scholar record). Full text pp. 427-439 not accessible.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. The quoted 'Findings' paragraph is present verbatim in (abstract field) and identically on the Emerald landing page and on p.427 of the publisher PDF I have now downloaded. So 'confirmed'. Status correction (a description exists but is not accessible -> statement found in an open source): the compilers missed the author's institutional repository. eprints.unmas.ac.id (Universitas Mahasaraswati Denpasar, full_text_status=public, no login) openly serves ALL the first-hand sources: (1) Arka, Kosmas & Suparsa 2007 'Bahasa Rongga: Tatabahasa Acuan Ringkas' (Glottolog's top grammar ref; eprint 682, 257-pp scan), (2) Suparsa 2008 Udayana dissertation 'Fonologi Baha…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress in Rongga is rule-governed/predictable (Suparsa treats it as P-rule 14 'penempatan tekanan', not lexical), assigned by syllable count from the word edge regardless of onsets; the abstract seems to say disyllables are stressed on the first (= penultimate) syllable but literally says 3-4-syllable words are stressed on 'the last syllable' -- which would be an odd split and is very likely a mistranslation (e.g. of 'suku kedua dari akhir'). The actual position cannot be fixed from accessible text; Arka 2016 section 4.3 'Tekanan dan Intonasi' or the Emerald full text is needed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Keywords list 'Primary, Secondary' (stress), implying the article distinguishes primary and secondary stress; no accessible detail.
new_statements.exceptions: None accessible. (Relevant background from Suparsa 2008: schwa /ə/ occurs only word-initially and -medially, never finally, and never in vowel sequences -- the kind of fact that conditions stress exceptions in neighbouring Lio, but no such statement is available for Rongga.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated over mono-, di-, tri- and quadrisyllabic words (citation forms); Rongga is isolating (no affixes), so word = root.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Rongga proper (ISO ror = rong1269), spoken in Tanarata, Watunggene, Bamo and Komba villages, Kota Komba district, Manggarai Timur, Flores; Suparsa's and Arka's data come from the same community (Arka's ELDP project 2004-06, Suparsa was a project member). Antonius et al. 1997 label the same variety 'bahasa Ngadha dialek Rongga' (i.e. as a Ngadha dialect); Suparsa 2008 and Arka argue it is a separate language. Little internal dialect variation is reported (Elias 2018:84).

new_statements.translation: p.44: "Rongga is not a stress language. Stress is not functionally phonemic. That is, the same word with stress on a different syllable does not give rise to a difference in meaning." p.45: "The word-stress pattern of Rongga is shown in (2-35). In general it can be said that primary stress is usually on the last syllable (2-35)a,c, except in disyllabic words, where there is usually variation, with stress usually on the first syllable, i.e. the second from the end (2-35)b. (2-35) ... a. Monosyllabic words: [σ'] (e.g. dhu' 'particle') b. Disyllabic words: [σ'σ] (e.g. bha'.bha 'angry') c. Words of three or more syllables: [(σ)σσσ'] (e.g. ga.ra.gem' 'sound of a dove', fa.ra.ge.ge' 'spider')"

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog stress on syllable 1 of 2, 3 of 3, 4 of 4, 5 of 5 (disyllables initial, three syllables and longer final) and as Suparsa's dissertation/2020 article (mono- and disyllables first syllable; tri- and quadrisyllables last). Adds: stress is non-phonemic ('not a stress language'), disyllabic placement is variable, compounds carry primary + secondary stress on their members. Also resolves the 'unclear or contradictory' reading assigned to the garbled Suparsa 2020 abstract in existing_statements: the intended rule is the same length-conditioned one.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-phonemic ('Rongga is not a stress language'), but in natural speech syllables are unequally prominent. Primary stress is usually on the last syllable of the word: monosyllables [σ'] (dhu'), trisyllables and longer [(σ)σσσ'] (ga.ra.gem' 'dove call', fa.ra.ge.ge' 'spider'); the exception is disyllables, which show variation and usually carry stress on the first (= penultimate) syllable, [σ'σ] (bha'.bha 'angry'). Four-syllable compounds do not show consistent stress: each member keeps its own stress and one becomes primary, the other secondary, in at least two patterns, [[σσ'][σ`σ]] (bhu.gu'.bha`.ga 'uproar') and [[σσ`][σ'σ]] (ghe.o`.gha'.o 'winding'). Acoustic correlates named: intensity, length, pitch.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only in compounds: p.45 'masing-masing kata pembentuknya ada tekanannya, dan salah satu menjadi tekanan utama kata majemuk bersangkutan, dan yang lainnya menjadi tekanan sekunder' (each constituent word keeps its stress; one becomes the compound's primary stress, the other secondary), patterns (2-36)a [[σσ'][σ`σ]] bhu.gu'.bha`.ga and (2-36)b [[σσ`][σ'σ]] ghe.o`.gha'.o, 'walapun harus diakui ada variasi yang lain' (other variation admitted).
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllables: initial stress is the usual pattern but 'biasanya ada variasi' (there is usually variation); four-syllable compounds 'tidak menunjukkan kosistensi tekanan kata' (show no consistent word stress). The whole system is hedged with 'biasanya' (usually) and stress is stated to be non-contrastive.
new_statements.identity_note: None of the works opened names a dialect; the 2007 grammar describes Rongga of Manggarai Timur (west-central Flores) as a single variety. Pastika 2019 labels its Rongga list 'Flores Barat'.

sources.citation: Suparsa, I Nyoman. 2008. "The Phonology of Rongga Language: a Transformational Generative Study / Fonologi Bahasa Rongga: Sebuah Kajian Transformasi Generatif" (Udayana dissertation summary, English + Indonesian). Linguistika: Buletin Ilmiah Program Magister Linguistik Universitas Udayana 15 (Sept 2008), 17 pp. [= Glottolog 313897 'E-Journal Universitas Udayana 2009']. Neliti 229701.
sources.note: Lists 14 phonological rules of which no. 14 is 'KF penempatan tekanan' (stress placement rule) and says '[tense] and [stress]' / 'Secara fonetis diperlukan ciri [tegang] dan [tekanan]' are needed phonetically -- i.e. stress is treated as rule-assigned (predictable), but the summary never states WHERE stress falls. Syllable canon V, CV; 6 vowels incl. schwa (no word-final schwa).
